newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia expects mixed markets for coming week.
newsitem.headline: Asia expects mixed markets for coming week.

text.p: Asian markets will be decidedly mixed in the week ahead, with Tokyo investors cautious before general elections and consolidation expected in Hong Kong.
The few markets with a positive outlook were Karachi, where shares may rise on good news from the International Montetary Fund, Manila and Seoul.
Expected decliners include Singapore, which may take a beating due to scarce positive economic news, and Thailand, which may fall slightly on lack of new incentives.
U.S. stocks rallied on Friday on retail sales and wholesale inflation data that indicate moderate economic growth, pushing aside concerns about quarterly earnings news.
The Dow finished up 48 on Friday at 5,969 but shed almost 24 points over the week.
TOKYO - Stocks are likely to remain in a limited range with investors cautious because of the general elections on October 20 and an unclear political climate, brokers said.
"Since there are no specific factors to inspire buying, the Nikkei is likely to be trapped between 20,500 and 21,500 next week," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities.
On Friday, the key 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,968.16, down from 21,148.03 a week earlier.
HONG KONG - Stocks are seen consolidating around newly gained ground in the week ahead as investors may become more cautious after the recent gains, brokers said.

The market needed a breather after the recent stellar performance, they said. While there is unlikely to be much downside, they said the blue-chip Hang Seng Index could fall 100 to 200 points before finding support at around 12,000 points.

But the market might also see further fund flows, which would push it higher, with possible upside at 12,400 to 12,500 points. The index ended last week at 12,218.40 points, up 312.89 points, or 2.63 percent, on the week.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are seen range-bound after prices bounced back from a sharp fall but lacked incentives to push ahead, brokers said.
Disappointing first half company results, though expected, would put pressure on prices, they said.
Petrochemicals giant Reliance is likely to see its net profits shrink 25 percent for the six months to September 30, when it announces its results on Friday, analysts said.
The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index rose 59.25 points or 1.91 percent to 3,160.52 after tumbling 153.46 points or 4.71 percent the week before.
COLOMBO - Sri Lanka stocks are expected to continue moving in a tight range in the absence of new factors, brokers said.
Turnover in the past week averaged about 30 million rupees, supported mainly by foreign buying of selected blue chips.
Retailers booked profit among cheap liquid shares, keeping the index in a tight range. The all share index closed at 591.41 on Friday, 0.92 points lower from a week earlier.
BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to fall slightly on the lack of fresh incentives to boost market investment, brokers said.
"The market has already tumbled heavily because of heavy selling by foreigners. They're expected to slow down selling this week," said Susheel Narula, head of research at Seamico Securities.
The SET index closed at 932.86 on Friday, compared to 1,004.89 the previous week.

DHAKA - A warning by the market watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for cautious trading halted a bull-run of Dhaka stocks, and analysts said the market will continue consolidating in the week ahead.
"The market badly needed a correction. The SEC has done the right thing," said one broker.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) benchmark index gained 238.16 points to 2024.43 in the week ending on Thursday.

JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are expected to be mixed with the focus remaining on vehicle manufacturer Astra International and cigarette maker Sampoerna, brokers said. The head of sales for one domestic major brokerage firm said the market is likely to stabilise in the coming week.

Brokers said speculative buying of Astra was likely to continue following reports that the Nusamba group to which Indonesia's President Suharto is linked is interested in buying a stake in the country's largest automobile manufacturer.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 571.23 points, against the previous week's close of 588.35 points.

KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are likely to open up on Sunday after the Friday-Saturday weekend on news the government has accepted IMF conditions for a resumption of payments on Pakistan's stalled standby loan, dealers said.

"People are oversold and the initial market reaction on this news will be positive," dealer Ali Asghar said. "But it is still not clear what steps the government will take. We expect some tough economic measures which will ultimately hit the market."
On Thursday, the Karachi 100-share index rose 10.13 points, or 0.75 percent, to end at 1,363.72 points, compared to 1,397.49 a week earlier. Losers led gainers 144 to 89.
KUALA LUMPUR - Buyers are expected to remain picky, nibbling selectively at Kuala Lumpur blue chips as they await further fresh factors, dealers said.

The Second Board index, meanwhile, could continue to make up ground after correcting from lofty levels. On Friday, the benchmark Composite Index rose 1.82 points to 1,140.74, while the Second Board added 7.61 points to 579.79.
"The market seems to be consolidating quite well," said Leong Yoon Siang of TA Securities' international division.
The Composite Index fell 9.44 points during the week.
MANILA - The Philippine bourse will stage a technical rally but its gains are likely to be limited due to uncertainty over the political situation, analysts said.

The stock market lost 5.0 percent or 157.76 points week-on-week to close at 2,973.59 due to the realignment of foreign funds and the ouster of Senate president Neptali Gonzales, who was closely allied with the government.
"We expect the market to challenge 3,000 points. It's cheaper than it used to be," said Saturnino Mejia of Guoco Securities.
SEOUL - Across-the-board buying interest is expected to push the Seoul stock market up to the 850 level, brokers said.
"There are many favourable factors surrounding the market," said Kim Duck-sun of Hyundai Securities. "But consolidation looks inevitable for the next rally."
Choi Bum, trader at C.S. First Boston, said: "The market is stabilised. Hope of an interest rate cut will push the market to the 850 level."
The composite stock index closed on Friday at 833.43, up 57.00 points or 7.34 percent from the previous Friday's 776.43.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said the Singapore market is likely to take a further beating given the lack of positive economic news.
"We will be focused on the non-oil export data. Much will depend on that," a dealer with a European bank said.
After falling below key support of 2,100 on Friday, the next support for the Straits Times Industrials Index is seen at 2,060-2,045.

Dealers said bearish projections for Singapore's third quarter gross domestic product growth were dampening sentiment. Most growth projections ranged between four percent and five percent, though a major European bank predicted only 1.8 percent growth.
On Friday, the Straits Times Industrials Index closed at 2,076.65, compared to 2,148.86 the previous week.
SYDNEY - Dealers said underlying sentiment for Australian shares remained positive, but market direction is expected to be set by Friday's U.S. inflation and retail sales data.
"Even though the market ignored the Dow's fall on Thursday it will be conscious of any big move that occurs on Friday," said Philip Toop, a dealer at Brisbane broker Lance Jones.
The key All Ordinaries index finished the week at 2,336.8, just 3.8 points short of its record closing high of 2,340.6. The index gained 21.3 points, or 0.9 percent, over the week.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to continue their consolidation due to a lack of market-moving factors to break the stalemate, brokers said.
Blue chips may get a boost from sound profit expectations as the October 31 deadline approaches for companies to release earnings reports for the first three quarters.
"I see slow trading again, with individual sectors seeing some performance based on their profit and sales figures for the first three quarters," said George Hou of Jardine Fleming.
On Friday the index closed at 6,582.00 points, compared to 6,616.21 a week earlier. A 6,500-6,650 range was seen for next week.

WELLINGTON - New Zealand's general election on Saturday has left financial markets in suspense over who will form the next government, but economists expect volatility to be limited when markets re-open on Monday.
The country's historic first election under a proportional voting system offered little fresh information to trade on, they said on Sunday.
A spokesman for ratings agency Standard and Poor's told Reuters the election result was "not terribly surprising" and that S&P was broadly comfortable with it.

Brokers said it appeared most investors would be comfortable with a centre-left, Labour-led government. Polls suggest Labour may be in a position to form a new government if it can seal a deal with the left-wing Alliance and nationalist NZ First.
The NZSE-40 index ended at 2,249.54, 5.26 points higher than last week's close and 25.22 points shy of an eight 8-1/2 year high of 2,274.76 posted on Monday.
